question: Top 10 Home Robots Hitting Shelves in 2028
body:
## Direct Answer For a general-purpose helper you could realistically welcome into a living room, the **1X Neo** is the best home robot pointed at 2028 shelves — it is the rare humanoid designed *home-first*, built lightweight and soft-skinned for safety around people rather than retrofitted from a factory arm. The strongest runner-up is **Tesla Optimus**, which trades Neo's consumer polish for manufacturing scale and a deep AI stack that could make it cheaper and more capable over time. Below them sits a wide field — from **Figure 03** and **Apptronik Apollo** to ambient companions like **Samsung Ballie**, plus the unglamorous task robots (lawn, pool, floor) that will almost certainly outsell every humanoid combined in 2028. The honest headline for anyone shopping this category is that 2028 is the year home robotics stops being a CES sizzle reel and starts being a shipping product line — but unevenly. A handful of humanoids will arrive as small, expensive, early-access units; a much larger wave of purpose-built robots will quietly become mainstream appliances. This guide ranks the ten machines most likely to actually reach a driveway, kitchen, or floor in 2028, separates the reservations from the retail, and explains where each one earns its keep. We deliberately avoid inventing prices and specs for products that vendors haven't finalized — where a number isn't public, we say so. ## How we chose We built this list around one uncomfortable question: *will you be able to buy it and use it in 2028, or are you buying a place in line?* That distinction matters more than raw capability, because the flashiest demos on the internet belong to robots that are years from a doorstep. Our ranking weighs five things. **Availability reality.** A real ship window, a stated consumer channel (not just enterprise pilots), and evidence of manufacturing capacity. A robot that only exists as a paid reservation is scored down, however impressive the reel. **Task usefulness in a real home.** Does it do work a household actually wants done — folding, tidying, mowing, vacuuming, pool cleaning, companionship — reliably and unsupervised? A generalist that does ten things at 60% is often less useful than a specialist that does one thing at 99%. **Safety around people and pets.** Weight, materials, force limits, and failure behavior. A 130-pound rigid humanoid and a 3-pound soft companion are not the same risk profile, and a home is not a fenced factory cell. **Total cost of ownership, not sticker price.** Hardware, subscription fees, teleoperation reliance, repairs, and the quiet truth that many early humanoids lean on remote human operators for hard tasks. We flag that dependency wherever it's known. **Ecosystem and support.** Firmware updates, app maturity, privacy posture on always-on cameras and mics, and whether the company is likely to still be shipping updates in 2030. For a broader framework on scoring emerging-hardware bets before they're proven, see our [buyer's-risk model for pre-release tech](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pre-release-hardware-risk-model). We did not rank by hype, funding, or valuation. Several of the best-funded humanoid companies land mid-pack here precisely because their 2028 product is a limited early-access unit, not a shelf item. ## The humanoid wave finally reaches the driveway The story everyone wants is the humanoid — a bipedal robot that walks into your kitchen and unloads the dishwasher. For 2028, four names dominate that conversation, and they are not interchangeable. **1X Neo** earns our top spot because 1X made the unusual choice to design for the home first. Neo is engineered to be lightweight and soft — a knit outer layer, tendon-driven limbs, and force characteristics meant to make a bump survivable rather than dangerous. 1X has publicly positioned Neo as a consumer product with early home deployments, and that consumer intent, more than any single spec, is what separates it from factory-born rivals. The known caveat, which 1X has itself discussed, is that early units lean on remote human operators to complete difficult tasks — so a 2028 Neo is best understood as a supervised assistant that improves as its autonomy grows, not a fully independent butler on day one. **Tesla Optimus** is the runner-up and the wildcard. Tesla's advantages are structural: in-house actuators, a shared autonomy stack with its vehicle program, and manufacturing muscle that could drive cost down faster than any competitor if production ramps as promised. Optimus has appeared in progressively more capable demonstrations, but Tesla's own timelines have moved, and much of 2028's volume is expected to serve Tesla's factories before it serves living rooms. Buy the story here on scale and price trajectory, not on guaranteed consumer availability. **Figure 03** and **Apptronik Apollo** round out the serious humanoids, and both are, candidly, enterprise-first. Figure has focused on commercial and logistics deployments and a proprietary AI model for manipulation; Apptronik's Apollo is a modular industrial humanoid backed by major manufacturing partners. Either could seed a prosumer or home-adjacent unit by 2028, but their center of gravity is the warehouse and the factory floor. They make this list because their technology sets the ceiling the home models chase — and because their pricing and reliability data will shape what a "reasonable" home humanoid costs. **Unitree G1** is the value entry and the honest outlier: a compact, comparatively affordable humanoid already sold to developers and enthusiasts. It is not a polished domestic helper — it's a capable platform for tinkerers, researchers, and early adopters who want to program their own tasks. If your definition of "home robot" includes "something I can actually own and hack on in 2028 without a five-figure enterprise contract," Unitree is the pragmatic pick. The diagram below shows how these five sort along the two axes that actually decide 2028 purchases — home-readiness versus general capability. ```mermaid quadrantChart title Humanoids for the 2028 home x-axis "Enterprise-first" --> "Home-first" y-axis "Narrow / early" --> "Broadly capable" quadrant-1 "Home-ready generalists" quadrant-2 "Capability leaders" quadrant-3 "Early platforms" quadrant-4 "Consumer newcomers" "1X Neo": [0.82, 0.62] "Tesla Optimus": [0.55, 0.80] "Figure 03": [0.28, 0.78] "Apptronik Apollo": [0.22, 0.70] "Unitree G1": [0.60, 0.30] ``` The takeaway: nobody is yet in the top-right "home-ready generalist" corner, which is exactly why humanoids remain early-access in 2028. Neo is closest on the home axis; Optimus and Figure lead on capability. Anyone promising you both, at consumer price, on a 2028 shelf, is selling optimism. ## Purpose-built beats general-purpose — the robots that will actually sell Here is the contrarian core of this list: the best-selling "home robots" of 2028 will not be humanoids. They'll be single-purpose machines that already work, priced like appliances, that a normal household buys without a second thought. Underrating these is the most common mistake buyers make when the humanoid narrative dominates the headlines. **Robotic lawn mowers** are the quiet breakout. Boundary-wire-free, GPS-and-vision-guided mowers from **Segway Navimow** and **Husqvarna Automower** have matured to the point where installation is trivial and mowing is genuinely hands-off. For homeowners with a yard, a 2028 mower delivers more recovered time per dollar than any humanoid on this page, and it does so unsupervised, in the rain, at night. This is the category where "robot that gives you your weekend back" is already true rather than aspirational. **Robotic pool cleaners** — led by cordless brands like **Aiper** — are the same story on a smaller footprint. Modern units navigate the pool intelligently, climb walls, and dock or surface themselves for retrieval. If you own a pool, this is a near-guaranteed satisfying robotics purchase in 2028, and it competes for household budget directly with the flashier machines above. **Floor robots** remain the anchor of the whole category. The next generation of **iRobot Roomba** and rivals like Roborock have pushed into arm-equipped models that pick up small objects, self-empty, self-wash mops, and map multi-floor homes reliably. The floor-care robot is the beachhead product — the machine that taught households to trust an autonomous device roaming the home — and it will remain the top-selling "robot" by units for the foreseeable future. The reason these win in 2028 is structural, and it's worth understanding before you spend: a narrow task in a constrained environment is a *solved* engineering problem, while general manipulation in an unstructured home is an *open* one. The chart below maps that trade-off — the further right a robot's job sits toward "open-ended manipulation," the less likely it is to work unsupervised in 2028. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[What do you want done?] --> B{Constrained,
repetitive task?} B -->|Yes| C[Floor, lawn, pool,
window cleaning] C --> D[Buy now — mature,
unsupervised, appliance-priced] B -->|No| E{General manipulation
in living space?} E -->|Yes| F[Humanoid helper] F --> G[Early-access in 2028 —
expensive, supervised, evolving] E -->|Ambient / social| H[Companion & home-hub robots] H --> I[Available, but value
depends on the software] ``` If your goal is recovered time and reliability, the left branch is where 2028's real value lives. The right branch is where the future is being built — thrilling, but you are funding a beta. A deeper breakdown of where autonomous task robots pay back fastest lives in our [task-automation ROI guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/home-task-automation-roi). ## The ambient home layer — companions, hubs, and rolling assistants Between the humanoids and the task robots sits a third category that's easy to dismiss and easy to overpay for: the ambient robot. These machines don't fold laundry or mow grass; they move around your home as a mobile screen, camera, speaker, and increasingly an AI companion. **Samsung Ballie** is the standout here — a small, rolling, ball-shaped robot that follows you around the house, projects displays onto walls, manages smart-home devices, and acts as a conversational assistant. Samsung has shown Ballie repeatedly and moved it steadily toward release, and with a mature large-language-model assistant behind it, Ballie is the most credible "AI companion that physically exists in your home" heading into 2028. Its value stands or falls almost entirely on the software — the hardware is charming, but a companion robot is only as good as the assistant driving it. **Amazon Astro's** next generation carries the same promise with Amazon's ecosystem behind it: home monitoring, patrol routines, Alexa integration, and the ability to check on rooms, pets, or elderly family members while you're away. Astro's clearest, most defensible use case is presence and security — a mobile camera that goes where a fixed one can't. That's a real job, and one many households will pay for. **LG's home robot** line (shown under names like CLOi and the Q9 mobile hub) rounds out the ambient tier: a legged or wheeled home assistant that greets, reminds, monitors, and controls connected appliances, leaning on LG's smart-home footprint. Like Ballie and Astro, its ceiling is defined by how good its AI feels day to day, not by what its brochure lists. The buying caution for this entire layer is privacy. An ambient robot is, by design, an always-present camera and microphone that moves through your most private spaces. Before you buy one, read the data policy, understand what's processed on-device versus in the cloud, and check whether recordings are retained or used for training. We treat that as a first-class purchase criterion, not fine print — our [connected-home privacy checklist](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/connected-home-privacy-checklist) walks through the specific questions to ask any vendor before a robot with a camera rolls into your bedroom. ## What actually ships in 2028 vs. what's a reservation The single most important thing to get right as a 2028 buyer is the difference between *retail* and *reservation*. The category is deliberately blurry about this, because a pre-order headline generates the same excitement as an in-stock one while committing the company to far less. Treat the task robots — floor, lawn, pool, window — as genuine retail. They have real inventory, real return policies, and years of shipping history. If a 2028 model is announced with a price and a ship date from an established brand, it's a normal appliance purchase. Treat the humanoids as reservations first, retail second. Even the most consumer-focused humanoid programs are expected to begin with limited, invitation-style, or waitlisted home deployments in 2028, often in specific regions, sometimes with a monthly service component and remote-operator support baked in. That is not a knock — it's the normal shape of a first-generation, safety-critical product. But it changes what you're buying: not a finished appliance, but early access to a platform that will get materially better through software over the following years. Budget for that reality, and don't assume a viral demo equals same-week shipping. The ambient robots fall in between — real products with real ship dates, but whose usefulness is gated by AI software that continues to evolve after purchase. You're buying capable hardware and a *promise* about the assistant. Weigh the company's track record on delivering software updates as heavily as the spec sheet. A practical rule for 2028: **if it cleans one thing in a bounded space, buy it now; if it walks and does everything, get on the list and keep your expectations calibrated to a first-generation, supervised product.** Following that rule alone will prevent the most expensive disappointment in the category. ## Price, safety, and the reality check Because we won't fabricate figures for products vendors haven't finalized, here's how to think about cost rather than a false table of prices. Task robots span from modest to premium appliance pricing and are generally a one-time purchase with occasional consumables. Ambient companion robots sit in premium-gadget territory and may carry subscription fees for cloud AI features. Humanoids are the wild card: early home units are expected to be expensive, and some programs may use a service or subscription model rather than an outright sale, partly to fund the remote-operator support that early autonomy still requires. Where a specific price isn't officially published, assume the marketing number and the delivered, all-in cost are different — and wait for independent reviews before committing. Safety deserves the last and loudest word. A soft, lightweight companion or a low-slung floor robot poses minimal physical risk. A full-size humanoid weighing over a hundred pounds, moving through a home with children, pets, and stairs, is a genuinely different proposition — and the industry knows it, which is why home humanoid rollouts are cautious, gated, and often supervised. When you evaluate any 2028 humanoid, ask three concrete questions: How much does it weigh and what happens if it falls near a person? Are its joints force-limited to yield on contact? And how much of its "autonomy" is actually a remote human operator? The answers separate a thoughtful product from a demo dressed up as one. Our overall guidance stands: for the widest set of households, the highest-value robotics purchases in 2028 are the boring, brilliant task robots — a mower, a pool cleaner, an arm-equipped vacuum — that reliably hand you back hours today. If you specifically want a general-purpose humanoid and you understand you're buying a first-generation, supervised, evolving product, **1X Neo** is the most home-considered choice, with **Tesla Optimus** the runner-up to watch on price and scale. And if you want the future to physically hang out with you, an ambient robot like **Samsung Ballie** is the most fun bet — just read the privacy policy first. ## Related questions ### Are home humanoid robots actually useful in 2028? Partially. Expect supervised assistants that handle tidying and simple chores, often with remote-operator help for hard tasks. They improve via software, but they aren't independent butlers yet. ### What's the best-value home robot for 2028? A robotic lawn mower or pool cleaner. Both work unsupervised, are appliance-priced, and recover more real hours per dollar than any current humanoid. ### Do home robots record video and audio all the time? Ambient robots like Ballie and Astro are camera- and mic-equipped by design. Check what's processed on-device versus in the cloud and whether recordings are retained or used for training. ### Will I be able to just buy a humanoid off a shelf in 2028? Mostly no. Early humanoid home units are expected to ship as limited, waitlisted, or invitation-based deployments, sometimes with a subscription and remote-support component, rather than open retail. ### Which company is furthest ahead on a home humanoid? 1X is the most home-focused with Neo; Tesla leads on manufacturing scale with Optimus; Figure and Apptronik lead on raw capability but target enterprise first. ## FAQ **Is the 1X Neo a fully autonomous robot?** Not entirely at launch. 1X has said early Neo units rely on remote human operators to complete difficult tasks, with autonomy expanding over time through software updates. Treat a 2028 Neo as a capable supervised assistant, not a hands-off butler. **How much will a home humanoid cost in 2028?** No universal figure is confirmed, and prices haven't been finalized across vendors. Expect early home humanoids to land in expensive, premium territory, and some may use a subscription or service model rather than an outright purchase. Wait for official pricing and independent reviews before committing. **Are robotic lawn mowers and pool cleaners really "robots"?** Yes — they're autonomous, navigate their environment with GPS and vision or sonar, make decisions, and complete tasks unsupervised. They're the most mature, highest-satisfaction robots most households will actually own in 2028. **What's the difference between Amazon Astro and Samsung Ballie?** Astro leans into home monitoring, patrol, and security with Alexa integration; Ballie is a rolling AI companion that projects displays, manages smart-home devices, and emphasizes conversation. Astro is about presence; Ballie is about companionship and control. **Do I need Wi-Fi or a subscription to use a home robot?** Most connected and ambient robots need Wi-Fi, and some cloud AI or monitoring features may require a subscription. Many task robots (mowers, vacuums, pool cleaners) perform their core job locally without a paid plan, though app features may need connectivity. **Are home robots safe around kids and pets?** Small companions and floor robots pose minimal risk. Full-size humanoids are heavier and warrant more caution — look for force-limited joints, lightweight or soft construction, and clear fall-behavior information. The industry's cautious, supervised humanoid rollouts reflect exactly this concern. **Can these robots fold laundry, cook, or clean dishes?** General manipulation like folding and loading dishwashers is the hardest open problem in the field. Humanoids demo these tasks, but reliable, unsupervised performance in a real home is not guaranteed in 2028. Specialized appliances remain more dependable for now. **Should I buy a home robot in 2028 or wait?** Buy task robots now — they're mature and immediately useful. For humanoids, only buy if you understand you're getting a first-generation, supervised, evolving product; otherwise, getting on a waitlist while the technology and pricing settle is the lower-risk move. ## Sources - [IEEE Spectrum — Robotics](https://spectrum.ieee.org/robotics) - [The Verge — Robots & AI](https://www.theverge.com) - [MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com) - [Reuters — Technology](https://www.reuters.com/technology/) - [TechCrunch — Robotics](https://techcrunch.com) - [Wired — Gear](https://www.wired.com/category/gear/) - [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com) - [Consumer Technology Association (CES)](https://www.ces.tech) ## Related on PULSE - [Pre-release hardware risk model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pre-release-hardware-risk-model) - [Home task-automation ROI guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/home-task-automation-roi) - [Connected-home privacy checklist](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/connected-home-privacy-checklist) - [Buyer's guide to first-generation smart devices](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/first-gen-smart-device-buyers-guide)
